'''John Stewart Waugh''' (April 25, 1929 – August 22, 2014) was an American [[chemist]] and [[Institute Professor]] at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]].<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_a87AAAAMAAJ&q=%22Waugh,+John+Stewart%22+AND+%221929%22 |title=Who's who in Frontiers of Science and Technology - Google Books |date=2007-07-25 |publisher=Marquis Who's Who |access-date=2014-08-24|isbn=9780837957029 }}</ref> He is known for developing average hamiltonian theory and using it to extend NMR spectroscopy, previously limited to liquids, to the solid state. He is the author of [[ANTIOPE]], a [[freeware]] general purpose [[Microsoft Windows|Windows]]-based simulator of the [[spectrum|spectra]] and dynamics of [[nuclear magnetic resonance]] (NMR). He has also used systems of a few coupled [[Spin (physics)|spin]]s to illustrate the general requirements for equilibrium and [[ergodicity]] in isolated systems.

In 1974 Waugh was elected as a member of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]] (NAS), in the Chemistry section.<ref>NAS (2007)</ref>

Waugh was awarded the [[Wolf Prize in Chemistry]] for 1983/84 with [[Herbert S. Gutowsky]] and [[Harden M. McConnell]] for their independent work on [[NMR spectroscopy]].<ref name="Wolf">Wolf Foundation Prize Committee for Chemistry (n.d.)</ref> Waugh was cited for his "fundamental theoretical and experimental contributions to high resolution nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy in solids."<ref name="Wolf"/> In 2011, Waugh received the [https://news.mit.edu/2011/waugh-award-0512 Welch Award in Chemistry] for revolutionizing NMR spectroscopy. In the words of Ernest H. Cockrell, chair of the [https://www.welch1.org/ Welch Foundation], Waugh "discovered how to use NMR to study solids, creating a collection of tools that allows researchers to view the structures and properties of proteins, membranes, viruses, and many other critical components of life." His work continues to be used extensively in chemistry, physics, biology, materials science, and medicine. He died on August 22, 2014.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://newsoffice.mit.edu/2014/john-waugh-obituary |title=John Waugh, Institute Professor emeritus, dies at 85roa &#124; MIT News Office |date=22 August 2014 |publisher=Newsoffice.mit.edu |access-date=2014-08-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140824071855/http://newsoffice.mit.edu/2014/john-waugh-obituary |archive-date=2014-08-24 |url-status=live }}</ref>

His father, [[Albert Waugh]], was a professor of economics and statistics at the [[University of Connecticut]], where he also served as provost for fifteen years.<ref name=":2">{{Cite news |date=1985-03-08 |title=Albert E. Waugh, 82; Retired UConn Provost, Vice President |work=The Hartford Courant |id={{ProQuest|758764934}}}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Griffin |first=Robert G. |date=2015-09-01 |title=John Stewart Waugh |url=https://physicstoday.aip.org/obituaries/john-stewart-waugh |access-date=2025-10-23 |website=[[Physics Today]] |language=en}}</ref>
